desc:
Each cell of the rectangular grid is either a wall, written -1, or a free cell holding that many coins (0 or more). A walker starts in the top-left cell and wants to reach the bottom-right cell, moving only one step right or one step down and never stepping onto a wall. The walker picks up the coins of every cell it stands on, including the first and the last one.

Return the largest number of coins that can be collected on a valid walk, or -1 if the bottom-right cell cannot be reached at all (this includes the case where the start or the destination is a wall).
hints: Without walls this is a plain maximum path sum: the best walk into a cell extends the better of two neighbouring walks. What changes when a neighbour is a wall or unreachable?
Let best[r][c] be the most coins on a valid walk ending at (r, c), with -1 meaning that no valid walk ends there. Coins are never negative, so -1 can never be mistaken for a real total.

For a free cell, take m = max(best[r-1][c], best[r][c-1]) (missing neighbours count as -1). If m is still -1 the cell is unreachable, otherwise best[r][c] = m + grid[r][c]. The start cell is seeded with its own coins.
editorial: The structure is the familiar right/down grid DP, with one extra state: unreachable. A cell can be entered from above or from the left; the better of those two walks should be extended. Walls are simply never entered, so their best value is forced to -1, and a free cell whose two predecessors are both -1 becomes -1 as well.

Because every real total is at least 0, the value -1 is a safe marker, and a maximum over predecessors naturally prefers any real walk to a missing one. Using a single array that is updated row by row gives O(m · n) time and O(n) space. The answer is the last cell's value, which is already -1 when the destination is a wall or unreachable.
